title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Boston, MA: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Boston-area welders and QC staff: building code, gas utility, lab piping and shipyard work, and which Part C code to pick.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Boston: Six Days to Get Ready for the Welding Inspector Exam Across New England's Mixed Codes
html:
Few metro areas ask a welding inspector to switch codes as often as Greater Boston does. One week the job is structural steel on a lab building in the Seaport, the next it is a gas main replacement in a suburb, then a stainless process line inside a pharmaceutical plant, then a weekend call from a shipyard an hour up the coast. The AWS Certified Welding Inspector credential is the common thread employers look for across all of it. Atlantis NDT runs a six-day CWI exam-preparation course (a 6-day program) for Boston-area welders, pipefitters, QC technicians, NDT technicians and engineers getting ready to sit the AWS examination.

Atlantis prepares candidates and does nothing more official than that. The American Welding Society runs the CWI examination, scores it and grants the certification, and AWS has not approved, accredited or endorsed this course. Eligibility, the vision test and the application are matters between each candidate and AWS. For the complete day-by-day syllabus and the published exam structure, see the AWS CWI exam prep course page.

A region built on many codes

Boston's welding work is spread across sectors that each answer to a different rulebook. That matters for a CWI candidate because the examination asks you to pick a single code book for Part C, while a working inspector here may touch three or four over a year. Understanding which code governs which job is part of what makes an inspector valuable locally.

  • Commercial and institutional buildings follow the Massachusetts State Building Code and, for structural steel welding, AWS D1.1.
  • Highway and transit structures owned by MassDOT and the MBTA bring in the AWS bridge code and agency specifications.
  • Natural gas distribution and transmission work is welded and accepted under API 1104, with federal pipeline safety rules sitting above it.
  • Biotech, pharmaceutical and semiconductor plants run on process piping built to ASME B31.3; qualification of welders and procedures there follows Section IX of the ASME boiler code.
  • Naval and commercial shipbuilding in the wider region follows Navy and classification requirements on top of welding codes.

The sections below take each of these in turn and explain where a CWI earns a living in it.

Steel buildings and the Massachusetts State Building Code

The Massachusetts State Building Code, published as 780 CMR, builds on the International Building Code with state amendments. Its special inspection provisions mean that structural welding on permitted projects is checked by qualified inspectors working for the owner rather than for the steel contractor. Testing and inspection agencies across Greater Boston employ CWIs for exactly this work: verifying that welders are qualified, that procedures are followed, that fillet sizes and groove profiles match the drawings, and that the welds meet D1.1 acceptance criteria.

Laboratory and research buildings in Cambridge, the Seaport and the inner suburbs are heavy on steel framing, mechanical supports and rooftop equipment platforms, all of which generate structural welds. Fabrication shops serving those projects also need in-house inspectors to control quality before steel leaves the yard. If building work is your target, D1.1 is the natural Part C choice, and the AWS D1.1 overview and the D1.1 acceptance criteria guide are good places to start reading.

Bridge work is its own specialty. State and transit agencies use the AWS bridge welding code with their own contract provisions, and fabricators supplying girders and other bridge members expect inspectors who know how fracture control and member classification change the inspection plan.

Gas utilities, pipelines and API 1104

Massachusetts gas utilities have spent years replacing aging cast-iron and bare-steel mains, and that work keeps welders and inspectors busy across the region. On steel gas lines, federal pipeline safety rules in 49 CFR Part 192 point operators to API 1104 or ASME Section IX for qualifying welding procedures and welders, and API 1104 is the standard most pipeline crews and inspectors carry. A CWI who reads API 1104 confidently is useful to utilities, their contractors and the inspection firms that serve them.

The utilities also train their own people. The AWS Boston Section has scheduled a tour of the National Grid New England Welding Training Center, which the section describes as a 21,000-square-foot facility with more than 11,000 square feet devoted to welding. A training investment on that scale tells you how seriously the region's utilities take welding quality. For candidates whose experience is on pipe, choosing API 1104 for Part C usually makes the code questions feel like reading their own job; the API 1104 overview explains how the standard is organized.

Laboratories, pharmaceutical plants and high-purity piping

The life-science industry around Boston and Cambridge brings a kind of welding most CWI candidates elsewhere rarely see: thin-wall stainless tubing joined by orbital gas tungsten arc welding, where weld color, internal profile and documentation carry as much weight as strength. ASME B31.3 includes a chapter for high-purity piping, and owners in this sector usually layer the ASME Bioprocessing Equipment standard on top of it.

The CWI examination does not test hygienic tubing standards directly, but for process piping inspectors the nearest Part C fit is the ASME selection, where Section IX is examined together with the B31.1 and B31.3 piping codes. Candidates from this world tend to be strong on documentation and procedure control and weaker on structural topics such as fillet weld gauging and structural acceptance tables, so Part B practice deserves extra time. For background on how procedure and welder qualification fit together, read the WPS, PQR and WPQ explainer and the ASME Section IX overview.

Shipyards within driving distance

Boston itself is no longer a major shipbuilding city, but several large yards sit within commuting or weekly-travel range. Portsmouth Naval Shipyard in Kittery, Maine maintains Navy submarines. General Dynamics Electric Boat builds submarines in Groton, Connecticut and fabricates modules at Quonset Point, Rhode Island. Bath Iron Works builds destroyers on the Kennebec River in Maine. These employers and their suppliers pull welders, fitters and inspectors from across New England.

Navy work runs under NAVSEA requirements, and shipyards qualify their inspectors to those requirements in their own programs. A CWI is not a substitute for that qualification, but it is a personal credential that stays with the inspector between employers and gives a strong grounding in processes, discontinuities and measurement. Many inspectors who move between the submarine supply chain and civilian construction keep both.

Offshore wind adds a newer thread. Projects in federal waters south of Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket have been staged through New Bedford, and wind foundations, transition pieces and substation structures are large welded steel products with demanding inspection plans. Inspectors who understand structural welding codes and visual acceptance have a place in that supply chain.

Where New England welders come from

Massachusetts relies heavily on its regional vocational technical high schools to start welders young, and the AWS Boston Section stays close to them. The section's recent posts covered the Massachusetts SkillsUSA welding competition held at Blackstone Valley Regional Technical High School in May 2026, and a gold medal won by a student from Diman Regional Vocational Technical High School. The section also lists an AWS student chapter at SeaCoast School of Technology. Union apprenticeships for ironworkers, boilermakers and pipefitters add another route, as do the utilities' own training programs.

None of these produces a CWI directly. The certification sits several years down the road, after a welder has built enough documented, verifiable experience to satisfy AWS. AWS wants five years of welding-related work from a candidate whose schooling ended with a high school diploma; a welding or engineering technology degree shortens the wait, and the full education-versus-experience table is on the national course page. If you started in a vocational program, keep your shop records and certificates: they help when you describe your experience to AWS.

The AWS Boston Section is also where working inspectors meet. Its events, from facility tours to competition coverage, are listed at sections.aws.org, and talking to a few local CWIs about their practical exam is worth an evening.

Booking the exam from Boston

Two of the three exam parts are taken on a computer. Fundamentals (Part A) and code application (Part C) are scheduled through Prometric, using the eligibility code from your AWS confirmation letter, and Prometric operates test centers throughout eastern Massachusetts and New England. The practical (Part B) is separate: AWS holds it at selected seminar and examination venues on dates it sets, and you work with specimens and instruments AWS provides. Look up the nearest practical venue and its dates on aws.org early, because those dates rarely move.

AWS expects at least 72% on every part and reports the three results together. The vision test, covering near vision and color perception, must be done on the current AWS form before you sit. AWS lists its examination charges on aws.org; to build a full budget that includes study time, travel and the code book, use the CWI exam budget planner. The article on results by exam part explains where candidates typically struggle.

Fitting six days around a Boston workload

The course follows one outline whether you take it alone or with coworkers. Day one covers welding processes, AWS terminology, joint design and welding symbols. Day two covers metallurgy, mechanical testing, discontinuities and their causes, inspection methods, safety and inspector ethics. Day three prepares for the practical with measuring, gauging and visual acceptance. Day four works inside the code book. Day five is timed practice exams for all three parts, and day six turns the results into targeted review plus an exam-day and application checklist.

Studying alone

Individuals take the course online. The six days become a study plan you follow around shifts, supported by written materials, Atlantis-written practice questions, timed mock papers and an instructor you can message with questions. There is no timetable to keep. A pipefitter on a utility crew might cover a day of material across two or three evenings, while a lab-construction inspector between projects might move faster.

Training a team

Employers can host all six days at their own site for a group of employees. A testing agency, utility contractor or fabricator gets practice built around the gauges, weld samples and code book its inspectors actually use. Each person still applies to AWS personally and has to satisfy the experience and vision requirements in their own name.

Every practice question in the course is original and written to the published body of knowledge. None is a real AWS examination question, and nobody at Atlantis sees the real examination.

When your hours span several codes: choosing the Part C book

Boston inspectors often ask which book to choose when their work covers several. A few principles help:

If most of your hours go toLean towardKeep in mind
Building steel and special inspectionAWS D1.1Most transferable book for structural work across the region
Gas mains, services and transmission linesAPI 1104Short and focused, but its acceptance tables need careful reading
Process, utility and power pipingThe ASME choice (Section IX, B31.1, B31.3)More volume to navigate, so tabbing and index practice matter
Highway and transit bridgesAWS D1.5Useful if you work for bridge fabricators or agency inspection consultants

The examination edition AWS lists can be older than the newest edition in print, so check the AWS reference material before buying a book. Choosing the code you use daily usually beats choosing the one with the most prestige. AWS also offers additional code endorsements later, which is how many inspectors cover a second code after passing.

Beyond the CWI in Massachusetts

A CWI judges welds mainly by eye and by paperwork. Many Boston-area inspectors add nondestructive testing methods so they can also find what is below the surface: ultrasonic testing on structural and pipe welds, magnetic particle testing on steel, and liquid penetrant on stainless. Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, the employer certifies its own technicians after training, experience and examination. That is the stage where Atlantis's SNT-TC-1A-based courses come in: start with NDT training in Boston, VT Level 1 training and ultrasonic testing in Boston. For inspection services in the state, see inspection services in Massachusetts.

AWS treats the CWI as a nine-year credential: renewals are filed in the third and sixth years, recertification comes due in the ninth, and a current vision record has to be on file along the way. Some inspectors later pursue Senior CWI or move into quality management. For career context, read CWI requirements and career impact, and use the free NDT practice tests if you are also preparing for method certification.

Getting a quote for Boston-area candidates

Send a short note with the number of candidates, a summary of each person's education and welding experience, the Part C book each plans to choose, and whether anyone already has an AWS application or practical date in hand. For on-site delivery, add the site location, available gauges and weld samples, and the weeks that work around your project schedule. Send it with the enquiry form for Boston candidates, and we reply within one business day.

Elsewhere in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic, see CWI exam prep in New York, Philadelphia and Baltimore.

faq.q: Do you run CWI prep classes in Boston?
faq.a: There is no Atlantis classroom in Boston; the company's offices are in Houston and Hyderabad. Individuals study online with an instructor answering questions, and employers can host the six days at their own site. The outline is on the national course page.
AWS does. It sets and scores the examination and certifies the people who pass. Atlantis prepares candidates and has no role in the examination or in certification decisions.

faq.q: Which Part C code should a gas utility welder choose?
faq.a: Usually API 1104, because steel gas pipeline welding and acceptance are built around it. See the API 1104 overview.

faq.q: I inspect stainless process piping in a biotech plant. Which code book fits?
faq.a: Pick the ASME selection, Section IX plus the B31.1 and B31.3 piping codes; it sits nearest to your daily work. Hygienic tubing standards are not tested directly, so expect to spend extra time on structural fillet gauging for the practical.

faq.q: Does the Massachusetts building code require a CWI for structural welding inspection?
faq.a: Massachusetts requires special inspection of structural welding, and it is the building official who rules on inspector qualifications. In practice, the CWI is what most structural welding inspectors on those projects present.

faq.q: Where do Boston candidates take the practical exam?
faq.a: AWS holds Part B only at selected seminar and examination venues on dates it sets. Check aws.org for the nearest venue. Parts A and C are computer-based tests booked through Prometric.

faq.q: Can shipyard experience at Portsmouth or Electric Boat count toward eligibility?
faq.a: Welding-based work that you can document and that someone can verify may count; AWS makes the decision. List your roles, dates and duties rather than one block of years.

faq.q: Are the course practice questions from the real exam?
faq.a: No. Atlantis writes every practice question to the published body of knowledge and has no access to AWS examination content.

faq.q: Is there a local AWS section?
faq.a: Yes. The AWS Boston Section holds events such as facility tours and follows the state SkillsUSA welding competition. Its page is on sections.aws.org.
Course pricing is quoted per request. Use the Boston enquiry form; AWS lists its own examination charges on aws.org.
